reason: This book was built three days ago at the 09-30 close and the week's news confirmed rather than contradicted it, so trading again would be churn I pay for twice. Leg-by-leg: (1) Managed care, my largest theme at 25% (CI 13 + CVS 12), got better not worse. CI reaffirmed 2026 adjusted EPS of at least $30.45 and a 10-14% growth target through 2030 at its Investor Day, Piper lifted its target to $370 on 10-01, BofA carries it as a top 2026 managed-care pick, and the sector bid on 10-02 as cost-trend hopes softened. At the $270.53 mark CI is 8.9x and CVS is ~10.8x the raised $7.90-8.10 guide. The 2027 setup is the thesis in one line: insurers are filing ~14% median marketplace premium increases against ~10% medical trend, which is pricing above trend and that is how MLR margin recovers. (2) Citi at $128.50 is 1.27x the $100.89 Q2 tangible book into 10-13 earnings, with consensus EPS +20.5% year over year and $30B of buyback running at roughly tangible book. That is a near catalyst I was positioned for on purpose, and selling ahead of it forfeits the reason I own it. (3) The XLP short is the leg the week strengthened most: the 10-year printed 5.34%, its highest since 2002, before easing to ~5.25%, and capital was actively leaving staples into energy and tech on 10-01. Short 21x bond proxies against a 5%+ risk-free is exactly the trade. (4) Pharma was neutral-to-positive, with a CAMZYOS pediatric label expansion and positive Phase 2 eczema data at PFE. Nothing is near a stop: the worst leg, PFE, is -2.52% against an 18% stop, and the book is only -0.20% weighted since entry, so no leg has become materially cheaper or richer than when I sized it. The one real flaw I found is worth recording rather than acting on. The energy stub (CVX 11 + XOM 8) and the XLP short are 30% of gross all leaning the same way on the Hormuz binary: a peace deal would drop oil from ~$100 and pull yields down, hurting both at once. That binary is genuinely live -- Trump said on 10-01 the war ends 'very soon, one way or the other', Qatar is mediating Iran's seven-day reopening proposal, and talks are called more serious. But I sized the damage and it is survivable, not existential: a deal costs roughly 2.6% of NAV across those legs against a 4.39% max drawdown to date, with no stop triggered, so risk management does not compel a trade. And both legs have standalone value cases independent of the macro -- XOM and CVX at 12.4-12.7x still earn at $80 Brent, and staples at 21x with no volume growth are a poor asset at any yield. Meanwhile OPEC+ is expected to hold output steady on 10-04 with ~5.7 mb/d still shut in through Q4, so the near-term supply picture supports the stub, and it is the only thing in an otherwise all-long book that pays if the war escalates into record-high index levels and a 5.3% 10-year. I would rather carry a deliberate stagflation tail hedge than strip it and be naked long defensives into an oil shock. Holding also keeps 14% cash earning 4% as dry powder for CI and BMY earnings on 10-29 and PFE on 11-03, which is when the next real information arrives. Deep value is paid for waiting through the holding period, not for re-underwriting a thesis every five sessions; the frictions and the rejection risk of rewriting a compliant eight-leg book are certain, and the expected gain from tinkering is not.
